title: Which armies can force mate
outcomes: Classifies bare-king armies as can or cannot force mate: rook, two bishops and bishop and knight can; one knight and two knights cannot
Tells two bishops on opposite colours from two on one colour, and a rook against a bishop from a rook against a bare king
Names the corner needed for bishop and knight: the colour of the bishop's squares

steps.text: Against a lone king some armies can **force mate** and some cannot. Can: queen, rook, two bishops on opposite colours, bishop and knight. Cannot: one bishop, one knight, two knights. 'Can' means the stronger side wins with best play; the tablebase confirms it for each position here. Test two armies first.

steps.caption: White to move mates in three. White has a dark-squared bishop; the corner h8 is a dark square.

line.say: A quiet move: the dark bishop heads for f6.
Black's king goes back to the corner.
Mate in the corner h8. The bishop gives check from a dark square, like h8.

claims.statement: Bg5 starts a forced mate in three.

steps.text: Check three things. Is the king really bare? With a rook against a bishop the result is often a draw, but not always: it depends where the kings stand, so check. Are the two bishops on opposite colours? With **bishop and knight**, the mate has to come in a corner of the bishop's colour. That is the textbook rule; this lesson checks it on one pair of positions.

steps.prompt: In the first position White can force mate within three moves. Now the bishop stands on a light square. Predict again.
